principles.statement: Gate authentic audiovisual input by learner × clip readiness, not by one global vocabulary count or CEFR label.
Use clip-specific estimated aural lexical coverage as a primary readiness feature; text-only vocabulary knowledge is weaker evidence for spoken-video access.
Treat approximately 95% lexical coverage as a research-informed candidate band for relatively stable listening/viewing comprehension, never as a universal unlock constant.
Do not use low lexical thresholds that permit content comprehension through imagery as proof of independent audio readiness.
Keep message understanding with video and audio-dependent understanding as separate evidence dimensions.
Record visual-semantic grounding because supportive imagery can lower pedagogical difficulty, but never let visual success silently update listening mastery.
Treat speech/playback rate as a learner-relative load feature rather than a universal WPM threshold.
Preserve speaker count, turn density, overlap/noise and connected-speech difficulty as separate readiness features until product data justify any aggregate weighting.
Weight unknown critical content words more heavily than raw unknown-token count when deciding whether a clip can carry the target message.
Use captions/subtitles as an explicit support state; success after answer-bearing text appears cannot be backfilled as independent listening success.
Analyze and unlock short windows within authentic sources rather than assigning one irreversible difficulty label to an entire video.
Recompute video readiness as learner aural vocabulary, listening evidence and support dependence change.
Use TV/movie corpus vocabulary profiles for candidate discovery and planning, not as individual learner mastery or clip-readiness evidence.
Keep lexical bands, speech-load weights, clip length and readiness-state boundaries falsifiable product hypotheses until EXP-009 validates them with Vietnamese near-A0 learners.
